306.t: How clubs pay for funerals and tax members
306.s: Clubs paid for funerals, taxing members and fining those who missed one.
306.q: Yeah. They paid the club, paid for the funeral. But see, members is taxed. They're taxed the members. That's when you don't have no food around the club, the society. I got only insurance. Whenever a member dies, I don't know nothing about it. But see, every time a member dies, now you pay so much,…

306.t: Clubs versus societies versus insurance companies
306.s: Rene compares what clubs, societies and insurance give members, and talks about insurance companies and banks.
306.q: Well, I think Balevalin is, they put you on the same basis. I tell you the reason why I say they're on the same basis. They give you, some give you a doctor in medicine, in the barrel, you know. Then a club, they might give you a, they'll bury it, they might give you a little sick, that's bad, they…

306.t: How social clubs and auxiliaries work
306.s: Rene explains social clubs, anniversary parades and expensive outfits, and how auxiliaries differ.
306.q: Well, auxiliaries separate. The auxiliaries mostly belong to these secret all to societies. Like they say, for instance, the L. Well, they have an auxiliarie. That auxiliaries are a bunch of men's or either women's in their drills, you see. They call that auxiliarie, you see. And they have a…

265.t: Who can join the club, and dues
265.s: Members are vouched for or investigated; dues are a dollar ten a month, with two meetings a month.
265.q: Well, we just, I mean, I got a good character and he's all right. I'm not a bad fella. There's always somebody vouch for him, you know.

265.t: Age limits, youngsters in the parade, pleasure fund and death fund
265.s: Members are 18 to 65; the Jolly Boys are for pleasure, with separate pleasure and death accounts.
265.q: But that's the rule. We have a lot of youngsters. Around 8, 7, 15, 16 years old, 13 years old, they parade with us. We don't charge them nothing to parade. All they do is just buy their parents, buy their clothes and they... We'll have maybe eight to ten youngsters, brothers like that. All up. They…

630.t: Social clubs he belonged to and which declined
630.s: He lists the clubs he belonged to while in the ballroom business, which ones went down, and the Zulus, Bethlehem and Eclipse.
630.q: Mmhmm. Eclipse Aiden Pleasure Club. Frogs. I used to be back at the National Park on Willow in Thuid. I belong to the, used to belong to the bulls. I used to belong to the money wasters. The original spokes. Oh I, uh, Zulus. Yeah Tammany. I used to be in all them things when I had some money. And…

630.t: Richest and oldest societies and halls sold out
630.s: They discuss societies losing halls and money, the Sanchez Center, the Bulls and a stolen treasury.
630.q: Well you got me there now. I wonder. I wonder. Some of them are going down. I don't know. I don't know which is the richest one now. I don't know.

862.s: Societies are for sickness and burial benefit, clubs for pleasure; examples of each are sorted out.
862.ch: Decline of funeral bands and societies
862.q: Well, what you see, with the club, it's more for pleasure, you see. Mm-hmm. And society is more for you, you know, being sick, you see.

567.t: How club members dressed for parades
567.s: Club men wore a white shirt, black pants, black tie and cap for parades.
567.ch: Funerals, dances and the end of the parades
567.q: White, white, uh, what, black, black shirt. That's it for, for, for funeral, what you mean? For parade? For parade, the guys in the clubs. Oh, what, for, for parade? Have white, alright. They have a white shirt, black black pants and a black tie. And what they, what they kept, you know what I mean?…

254.s: They talk about social clubs like the Dewey, the Tulane Club and the Durant, which lacked death or sick benefits and kept men and women separate.
254.ch: Reel 2: carnival, Prohibition, funerals and clubs
254.q: Oh, near where the Tulane Club is. The Tulane Club and the Durant, they're all both up around the same place. Oh, they're around the same place. I know where you're talking about. They're all the same neighborhood.

863.t: His social club and the San Jacinto Club
863.s: Buddy's small club meets house to house; he contrasts it with the big San Jacinto social and pleasure club with 1,500 members.
863.q: We don't have no club. Oh, you don't now. We meet from house to house. Oh, I see. Each member has a, a meeting. Uh huh. We got twenty, twenty standing members. And every month, once a month, every month he'll have a meeting, and the next member he'll have a meeting.

14.t: Union and society benefits, officers and outings
14.s: Love and Allen discuss officers, death benefits, sick pay and the annual outings of the union and the Young Men.
14.q: I forgot how much you get, but they paid something for the doctor bill. All that kind of business. When you keep the bucket, it was a matter of getting two, three hundred dollars. After they buried, you see, they paid for the bill. They'd give us three or four hundred dollars, something like that.

628.s: Williams lists the social and aid clubs he belongs to, such as the Greyhound club and the Garden District, and talks about funeral parades and the Young Men of Liberty's music.
628.q: I belonged to the Greyhound, they used to parade too, Greyhound sports. And the Garden District, they used to give a lot of dances and picnics and different things. And while the young man delivered, I was in there, otherwise they used it. Old man Bob, Bob, Bob, he was a member. He died in there,…

290.s: He joined no clubs, and sold insurance for Unity at one time.
290.q: You don't belong to them, you're not a big joiner? No, no, I don't belong to nothing like that. Did you ever belong to make insurances or...? Well I was, at one time, I used to be a salesman for Unity Insurance Company. Oh, I see. And then I was known widely from that, with the other companies too,…

798.t: Decline of organizations and parades; the 10th of May parade
798.s: Clark says old societies are dying out as youngsters do not follow, recalls big anniversary parades and the 10th of May parade.
798.q: Well not anymore. See, years ago, Young Men of Liberty used to use music. Perseverance used music. The charity used music. And there was another organization down there, Young Men's by Dave. But you see, Dick, in the later years, old men die out. That's it. The youngsters don't come behind. They…

298.s: Members of the lines club have dwindled and left Munster's for their own place.
298.q: A line between Annunciation and Chapitua. It's a place that they built. Oh, they built them on. That explains a lot. Yeah, they got their own club out there. Well, maybe that's why they went to town.

858.t: Clubs and societies he worked for and the decline of brass bands
858.s: He names clubs and societies he played for and says brass bands are not what they were.
858.ch: Brass bands and the WPA band
858.q: Clubs? Oh, yes. What are some of them that you work for? Oh, Tulane, the 80-30 Club, and, uh, the Valets, the Zulus, I played quite a few of them.
